summaries.example: Imagine a song that includes many instruments. The instruments are not the whole song, and the song is not just one instrument. In a similar comparison, panentheism says the world is in God and God is present in the world, while God and the world still remain different.
summaries.summary: Panentheism is a way of thinking about God and the world. Its name comes from Greek words meaning, roughly, “all in God.” Panentheists say that the world is in God and that God is active within the world. They also say that God is more than the world, so the world and God are not identical. This makes panentheism different from pantheism, which identifies God with the world. It also differs from classical theism, which strongly separates God from the world and usually says that the world cannot change God. Panentheistic thinkers disagree about what “in” means. It might mean that the world depends on God for its existence, that God and the world affect each other, or that the world is like a part within a greater whole. Some connect panentheism with ideas from science, such as emergence, where new features appear as parts work together. Others use ideas from process philosophy, in which God offers possibilities and the world responds. Critics ask whether this view makes God too limited or whether it is clear enough to differ from other views. Panentheists reply that their position protects both God’s presence and the world’s real importance and freedom.
key_ideas: Panentheism says that God and the world are closely connected.
It tries to keep two ideas together: God is present in the world, and God is more than the world.
Unlike pantheism, panentheism does not say that God and the world are exactly the same.
Many panentheists think the world can affect God in some way.
Different thinkers explain the connection between God and the world differently.
summaries.why_it_matters: Panentheism matters because it offers one way to think about God, nature, change, freedom, and suffering together. It can encourage people to see the natural world as deeply important without saying that nature is all there is. It also raises careful questions about how religious ideas and scientific ideas might fit together.

important_terms.definition: The view that the world exists in God, while God is also more than the world and the world is not simply identical with God.
God’s presence and activity within the world.
God’s being beyond or greater than the world, rather than being limited by it.
The view that God and the world are the same reality.
The view that God and the world are different, with God not being changed by the world.

questions_to_think_about: How is “the world is in God” different from “the world is God”?
Can something be part of a larger whole and still be different from that whole?
Would a God affected by the world be different from a God who never changes?
Which picture of the God-world relationship seems most understandable to you, and why?

summaries.example: Consider an evolving ecosystem. Its organisms depend on one another, and changes in one part can alter the whole system. Some panentheistic models use this kind of relational picture: the world is genuinely distinct, yet its history contributes to God’s ongoing life. The analogy is limited, because panentheism is making a metaphysical claim about God and reality, not merely describing a biological system.
summaries.summary: Panentheism is not one single doctrine but a broad group of proposals about the God-world relation. Its recurring idea is that the world is in God, God is present and active in the world, and God nevertheless exceeds the world. Many contemporary discussions add a reciprocal claim: the world affects God as God affects the world. This separates panentheism from classical theism, which usually treats God as ontologically distinct, immutable, and unaffected by created events, and from pantheism, which identifies God with the world. The word “in” is therefore crucial but ambiguous. It can express dependence for existence, participation in divine being, an emergent relation, a part-whole analogy, or a metaphysical relation of mutual influence. Historical anticipations have been identified in diverse philosophical and religious traditions, while the explicit term was used by Karl Krause in the nineteenth century. Modern forms developed especially through German Idealism, process philosophy, and reflection on evolutionary science. Process panentheism often portrays God as having an eternal aspect and a responsive aspect. God presents possibilities, but events in the world retain some self-determination; their actualizations then become part of God’s concrete experience. Other versions appeal to emergence: complex systems can display properties not reducible to their parts, potentially allowing higher-level or downward causation. Critics argue that this may weaken transcendence, fail to explain divine causal power, or make the appeal to God superfluous. Other critics claim that panentheism does not have a sufficiently stable definition. key_ideas: The central claim is that God includes the world, is present in it, and is more than it; many versions add that the world feeds back into divine life.
Panentheism seeks a balance between classical theism’s emphasis on transcendence and pantheism’s emphasis on immanence.
The meaning of “in” is disputed: it may refer to dependence for being, participation, mutual influence, emergence, or a metaphor such as part and whole.
Process versions often describe God as offering possibilities without determining every event, allowing finite events a degree of self-determination.
Some science-and-religion versions use emergence, systems, or entanglement to describe how divine action might be internal to nature rather than an external interruption.
Critics question whether panentheism limits divine power, makes divine causation unnecessary, or lacks a precise definition that separates it from neighboring views.
summaries.why_it_matters: The entry matters because it shows how a metaphysical position develops through arguments about ontology, causation, freedom, evil, science, and religious language. Panentheism also illustrates why definitions matter: saying that the world is “in” God can describe several importantly different theories. Studying those differences helps readers compare religious worldviews without treating any one version as representative of all of them.

important_terms.definition: A family of views holding that the world is included in God, while God is not exhausted by the world; many versions also hold that the world affects God.
God’s presence or activity within the world.
God’s being beyond the world or not limited by it. Panentheistic accounts interpret this in different ways.
A view identifying God and the world, or treating them as one reality, rather than preserving their distinction.
A form of theism emphasizing God’s distinction from the world, divine timelessness or immutability, and the world’s inability to alter God.
A relation in which each related reality can affect the other’s being or state; panentheistic accounts often apply this to God and the world.
The appearance of new properties or levels from organized combinations of elements; strong emergence treats these as genuinely new causal levels.
Causation in which a more complex level influences less complex elements, rather than all causation moving only upward from simpler physical parts.

questions_to_think_about: Does a mutual God-world relation require God to change in essence, or could only God’s experience change?
Can panentheism preserve both creaturely freedom and meaningful divine action?
Is emergence a scientific explanation, a metaphysical theory, or both in particular panentheistic proposals?
What definition of “in” best distinguishes panentheism from pantheism and classical theism?
If God does not control every event, how might a panentheist explain hope for the defeat of evil?

summaries.example: Think about a school orchestra. Each musician contributes to the performance, and the finished music is more than any one player. The players also change their timing when they hear the others. Some panentheistic ideas use a similar picture: the world is genuinely part of a larger divine reality, yet it is not the same as God, and the world’s history may affect God. The comparison is only a guide, not a proof.
summaries.summary: Panentheism is a family of views about how God and the world are connected. The name suggests that the world is “in God.” This does not mean that God and the world are identical. Instead, panentheistic thinkers generally maintain that God includes the world, is present in it, and is also more than it. Many versions add that the world influences God, creating a two-way relationship. This is a major difference from classical theism, which usually emphasizes God’s complete independence and says that events in the world do not change God’s being. Panentheism also differs from pantheism, which identifies God with the world. The difficult word is “in.” It might mean that the world depends on God in order to exist, participates in divine reality, or exists within a relationship in which God and the world affect one another. Some thinkers describe God as having an eternal aspect and a responsive aspect. In process philosophy, God presents possibilities to events, but those events make their own contributions rather than being completely controlled. This gives a role to freedom and helps explain why panentheists may not treat God as the direct cause of every evil event. Other thinkers use emergence, the development of new properties in complex systems, to explain how higher levels of nature might have real effects without denying physical processes. The idea has a long and varied history, with possible themes identified in several philosophical and religious traditions, and with the explicit label appearing in the nineteenth century. Critics say panentheism may limit God, blur the difference between God and nature, or fail to explain divine action. Some also argue that its many versions make it hard to define. key_ideas: Panentheism tries to hold together God’s closeness to the world and God’s greatness beyond it.
It differs from pantheism because the world is not simply identical with God.
It differs from classical theism because many panentheists say that the world can really influence God.
The word “in” can mean several things, including dependence, participation, mutual influence, or being part of a larger whole.
Process thinkers often say that God gives possibilities to events, but does not force every event to happen.
Critics and defenders disagree about divine power, human freedom, evil, and whether panentheism has a clear enough definition.
summaries.why_it_matters: Panentheism matters because it gives philosophers and theologians another way to discuss nature, God, freedom, and change. It can support the thought that the world is important to God without saying that the world is all of God. It also helps students see how one small word—“in”—can lead to major disagreements about reality.

important_terms.definition: The view that everything in the world is included in God, while God is greater than the world and not identical to it.
God’s presence and activity within the world.
God’s being beyond the world and not limited by it.
The view that God and the world are identical in reality.
A view that strongly separates God from the world and usually treats God as unchanging and unaffected by worldly events.
A two-way relationship in which God affects the world and the world affects God.
A new feature that arises when parts combine in a complex system, such as a property of a whole that is not found in each part alone.
The idea that a higher or more complex level can influence a lower or simpler level.

questions_to_think_about: Why might someone want God to be both beyond the world and present within it?
If the world changes God, does that make God weaker, or could it show that relationships matter?
How could emergence challenge the idea that everything can be explained only by tiny physical parts?
Can panentheism be clearly separated from pantheism if both say God is present in the world?
What problems might arise if God influences events but does not control them?
